screens.title: Voltage, Current, Resistance, and Ohm's Law
screens.narratorSegment: This chapter gives you the practical electrical vocabulary that makes embedded systems predictable and safe. You will learn what voltage, current, and resistance mean in physical terms, how Ohm's Law ties them together, and how resistors protect components like LEDs or translate voltages so sensors and microcontrollers can talk safely. We will use familiar examples — a single AA battery, the LaunchPad GPIO pins at 3.3 volts, and a USB five-volt supply — so you can map numbers to real hardware. You'll calculate currents through resistors, choose current-limiting resistors for LEDs, and build a simple breadboard circuit to measure voltages with a multimeter. That hands-on grounding prevents common mistakes like connecting an LED directly to a pin and risking damage. By the end of this lesson you will be able to compute voltage, current, or resistance from any two values, pick a safe resistor for an LED on a GPIO pin, and assemble and measure the circuit on a breadboard. Think of these skills as the electrical plumbing of your projects: they keep your system flowing without flooding the components.

keyIdea.title: Why this chapter matters
keyIdea.text: Voltage, current, and resistance are the foundational measures that determine whether your embedded circuit works and whether your components survive. Ohm's Law lets you compute safe values before you connect power.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: Over the next segment you'll gain four practical competencies. First, you will be able to define voltage, current, and resistance in clear physical terms and explain how they relate through Ohm's Law; this matters because correct definitions prevent confusion between pressure and flow when you wire circuits. Second, you will learn to calculate any one quantity when given the other two; this calculation skill is useful in choosing parts and verifying designs before powering hardware. Third, you will understand resistor roles in embedded circuits, including current limiting for LEDs and voltage division for level shifting; that knowledge prevents burned-out LEDs and incorrect sensor readings. Fourth, you will physically build the LED circuit on a breadboard and use a multimeter to measure voltages and confirm expected currents; this hands-on practice tests theory against the real world. Each competency includes a small visual mnemonic so you can recall the relationships quickly, and every card ends with a verified competency milestone so you know when you've mastered the skill.

screens.title: Learning Objectives (Hands-on focus)
screens.narratorSegment: These objectives emphasize hands-on application and safety. You will practice calculating resistor values for LEDs using real numbers from a 3.3 volt GPIO pin and typical LED forward voltages. You will also learn to create a voltage divider that scales a five-volt sensor output to a 3.3 volt microcontroller input, including an example using ten and twenty kilohm resistors. The goal is not only to compute numbers but also to understand when a voltage divider is appropriate and when you must buffer the signal instead. Another practical objective is breadboard wiring and measurement: you will connect ground rails and power rails reliably, use color conventions for wires, and use a multimeter to measure voltage across components, then compute current from those measurements. Finally, you'll learn to respect the GPIO pin current limit — for the LaunchPad family that means keeping single-pin currents under about eight milliamps unless otherwise specified, and choosing larger resistors when necessary. These practical skills reduce the chance of damaging LEDs or the microcontroller when you prototype.

screens.title: What is Voltage?
screens.narratorSegment: Voltage is the electrical potential difference between two points. Think of it as pressure in a water system: it is not the water flowing, but the push that can make water move when a path exists. In electronics we measure voltage in volts. Concrete examples help: a single AA battery typically supplies about 1.5 volts, the LaunchPad GPIO pins output 3.3 volts when HIGH, and a USB port provides 5 volts. Each of these numbers tells you how much potential energy per unit charge is available to move current through a component. A common misconception is to equate high voltage with high current — voltage is the driving force but only produces current when there is a path and a resistance. That distinction matters when you troubleshoot: a measured voltage at a pin does not guarantee a component will receive the expected current unless the circuit and resistor values are appropriate. In practice you use voltage to choose components and to determine expected drops across parts in series. For example, when driving an LED from 3.3 volts, we subtract the LED's forward voltage from the supply to determine how much voltage must appear across the resistor. Remember the water analogy: voltage sets the pressure, and it tells you how much potential there is to make things flow when the circuit is closed.

keyIdea.title: Voltage as pressure
keyIdea.text: Voltage describes potential energy per unit charge and sets the available 'push' that can drive current through components.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.1 › Voltage
Definition

Voltage is electrical potential

Voltage measures potential difference and acts like pressure. It determines how much push is available to move charge when a path and resistance exist.

Concrete examples
AA battery ≈ 1.5 V, LaunchPad GPIO HIGH = 3.3 V, USB power = 5 V. Use these numbers to plan resistor drops and expected component behavior.
Misconception check
High voltage does not automatically mean large current; current depends on the path and resistance present.
Key Takeaway

Voltage is the potential 'push' that can cause current; measure it before wiring to confirm compatibility.

Analogy
Water pressure analogy
Pressure in pipes is like voltage: it exists whether or not water flows. Flow requires an open path and depends on resistance.
Worked example
If a pin outputs 3.3 V and an LED forward voltage is 2.0 V, then 1.3 V must appear across the series resistor. That drives whatever current the resistor allows, computed with Ohm's Law.
Common mistake
Assuming the available current equals the voltage number. Always compute the current using the resistance in the circuit.

screens.title: What is Current?
screens.narratorSegment: Current is the movement of electric charge through a conductor and is measured in amperes, commonly called amps. A practical way to think about current is water flow in a pipe: it tells you how much charge passes a point per second. Components consume current according to how they're designed — a small LED might draw ten milliamps, while a motor can draw hundreds of milliamps or several amps. Embedded systems are sensitive to current because microcontroller pins can only source or sink limited amounts; for example, the TM4C123G GPIO pins used on many LaunchPad boards can safely provide around eight milliamps per pin. Exceeding that limit risks overheating the chip or causing unreliable behavior. When designing circuits, always compute expected current flows using Ohm's Law and compare them to component limits. One common misunderstanding is to confuse current with the capacity of a power supply: a supply's voltage is fixed, but its available current depends on its rating and what the connected circuit draws. Practically, measure voltage across a resistor and divide by resistance to compute current if you cannot measure current directly. That verification step keeps prototypes safe and predictable.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.1 › Current
Definition

Current is charge flow

Current, measured in amperes, tells you how much electric charge passes a point per second. Use the water-in-pipe analogy to keep this idea clear.

Concrete figures
Small LEDs: ~10 mA. Motors: hundreds of mA or more. GPIO pins: about 8 mA safe per pin on the TM4C123G family.
Measure indirectly
If you measure voltage across a resistor, compute current with I = V / R. This is often safer than trying to break the circuit to measure current directly.
Misconception check
Do not assume current is unlimited because voltage is present. Limits come from the path, resistances, and device ratings.
Practical example
If a 220 ohm resistor is connected to a 3.3 V pin, the current is I = 3.3 / 220 ≈ 0.015 A, or 15 mA. That is higher than the 8 mA safe guideline for a single TM4C123G GPIO pin, so you would choose a larger resistor or use a transistor driver to protect the pin.
Key Takeaway
Always compare calculated current with the device's safe current limit before connecting components directly to GPIO pins.
Quick checklist
  • Compute expected current with Ohm's Law.
  • Compare with per-pin and total device limits.
  • Use larger resistors or drivers when necessary.

screens.title: What is Resistance?
screens.narratorSegment: Resistance measures how much a component opposes current. It is expressed in ohms and implemented with resistors — small components with a fixed resistance rating. In embedded work resistors are indispensable: they limit current so LEDs and pins are not overloaded, they form voltage dividers to scale signals, and they provide pull-up or pull-down behavior for inputs. For example, if you want about ten milliamps through a red LED with a roughly two-volt forward drop from a 3.3 volt pin, you compute the resistor as R = (3.3 − 2.0) / 0.01 ≈ 130 ohms. Because standard resistor values exist, you often pick the next common value, such as 150 or 220 ohms, which reduces the current and increases safety. A frequent mistake is to omit the resistor and connect an LED directly; an LED on its own has very low resistance when forward biased, so it will draw uncontrolled current, often damaging the LED and possibly the microcontroller pin. Resistances in series add; in parallel they divide, which matters when arranging resistor networks. Remember that resistors protect both the device that supplies current and the device that consumes it, so always include them where the design calls for controlled current.

keyIdea.title: Resistance controls flow
keyIdea.text: Resistors set how much current flows for a given voltage. Use resistor calculations to protect LEDs and microcontroller pins.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.1 › Resistance
Definition

Resistance is opposition to flow

Resistors control current for predictable behavior. They are crucial when interfacing LEDs, sensors, and microcontroller pins.

Series resistor for LED
Example calculation: For a 3.3 V source and LED forward voltage 2.0 V, to obtain 10 mA use R = (3.3 − 2.0) / 0.010 ≈ 130 Ω. Choose a standard 150 Ω or 220 Ω to be safe.
Why use larger standard values
Picking a slightly larger resistor reduces current and protects pins when exact calculated values are not available as standard resistor sizes.
Common mistake
Connecting LEDs without a resistor lets the LED draw uncontrolled current and risks both LED and microcontroller damage.
Visual: resistor roles
Limit current
Series resistors set safe LED currents.
Divide voltage
Two resistors form a divider to scale voltages.
Pulls for inputs
Resistors can pull a pin to a known logic level when inputs are open.
Key Takeaway
Resistors make current predictable and protect both the source and the load. Use them intentionally.

screens.title: Ohm's Law and Solving for Unknowns
screens.narratorSegment: Ohm's Law is the practical formula that links voltage, current, and resistance: V = I × R. It also rearranges to I = V / R or R = V / I. To solve real problems, start by identifying the known quantities and converting units so they match — for example, convert milliamps to amps when necessary. A step-by-step approach keeps you from introducing arithmetic errors: 1) write the formula for the unknown, 2) substitute numeric values with correct units, 3) compute, then 4) confirm the result against component limits. Concrete example: with a 3.3 volt output and a 220 ohm resistor, compute current as I = 3.3 / 220 ≈ 0.015 A or 15 mA. Compare that to the microcontroller pin limit; if the pin limit is 8 mA, you must increase the resistor value or use a driver. Watch out for unit mismatches — 0.015 A is 15 mA, not 0.015 mA. Another common error is forgetting that a resistor in series with an LED must take the voltage difference between supply and LED forward voltage. Always perform a final sanity check: does the computed current align with expected brightness or device heat? That final check prevents costly mistakes on the bench.

keyIdea.title: Solve methodically
keyIdea.text: Use the correct arrangement of Ohm's Law, convert units, compute, and confirm results against device limits before wiring.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.1 › Ohm's Law
Process Flow

Solve V, I, or R in four steps

Step 1: Identify knowns
Decide which two of V, I, R you have.
Step 2: Choose formula
Use V = I × R, or rearrange to I = V / R or R = V / I.
Step 3: Convert units
Convert milliamps to amps and kiloohms to ohms before calculating.
Step 4: Verify limits
Compare computed current to pin and component limits; adjust resistors if needed.
Worked calculation
With V = 3.3 V and R = 220 Ω, I = 3.3 / 220 = 0.015 A = 15 mA. If your GPIO safe limit is 8 mA, this resistor is too small for direct connection.
Misconception
Don’t mix units. 0.01 A is 10 mA. Unit errors are common and can lead to selecting resistors that are far too small or too large.
Key Takeaway
Follow a method: pick formula, convert units, compute, and confirm limits to prevent hardware mistakes.

screens.title: Current-limiting Resistors for LEDs
screens.narratorSegment: When you drive an LED from a microcontroller pin, the resistor in series is the safety mechanism. The calculation uses the LED forward voltage and desired current: R = (Vsource − Vforward) / I. For example, with 3.3 volts from a GPIO pin and a red LED forward voltage around 2.0 volts, aiming for 10 milliamps gives R ≈ 130 ohms. In practice, pick the nearest common resistor value such as 150 or 220 ohms to reduce current slightly and preserve the pin. A key safety check is to compare the computed current to the microcontroller's per-pin limit — on some LaunchPad devices that limit is roughly 8 milliamps per pin. If the computed current exceeds the limit, increase the resistor value or use a transistor driver to source the LED current instead of the pin. Another point to compare is brightness versus safety: higher current makes a brighter LED, but pins and LEDs have thermal limits. A typical mistake is to assume any low-value resistor is fine because the supply voltage is small; even small supplies produce harmful current without proper resistance. Use the resistor to control current, verify by measuring voltage across it, and compute current using I = Vr / R to confirm.

keyIdea.title: Resistor selection matters
keyIdea.text: Calculate the resistor from supply and LED forward voltage, then choose a nearby standard value that keeps current within safe limits.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.1 › LED Resistor
Guideline

Compute, then choose standard value

Formula: R = (Vsource − Vforward) / I. Example: R = (3.3 − 2.0) / 0.010 ≈ 130 Ω. Use 150 Ω or 220 Ω as standard values to be safer.
Safety check
Compare computed I to the GPIO limit (≈8 mA for TM4C123G). If I is larger, increase R or use a driver transistor.
Key Takeaway
Selecting a slightly larger resistor value reduces current and protects both LED and pin.
Comparison: Direct vs Series resistor
Direct connection (wrong)
An LED connected directly to a pin will draw uncontrolled current, likely burning the LED or damaging the pin.
Series resistor (correct)
A properly calculated resistor limits current to a safe value and lets you predict brightness and power dissipation.
Check with a meter
Measure the voltage drop across the resistor and compute I = Vr / R to confirm the actual current when the LED is on.

screens.title: Voltage Dividers and Level Shifting
screens.narratorSegment: A voltage divider is two resistors in series that produce an output voltage equal to the input scaled by the ratio of the lower resistor to the total: Vout = Vin × (R2 / (R1 + R2)). It’s a simple and common way to step a 5 volt signal down to 3.3 volts so a microcontroller input isn’t overdriven. For example, selecting R1 = 10 kilohms and R2 = 20 kilohms with a 5 volt input yields Vout = 5 × (20k / (10k + 20k)) = 5 × (20/30) = 3.33 volts, close to the 3.3 volt target. When using dividers, be mindful of the input impedance of the receiving pin and any dynamic behavior of the sensor: voltage dividers present a finite output impedance that can be loaded down by low-impedance inputs or by sampling circuits at high speed. For sensors that drive significant current or require accurate timing, buffer the divider output with an op-amp or a voltage follower. A common misconception is to assume a divider can power a load — dividers are for signal scaling, not supplying current. Always measure the scaled voltage with a meter before connecting to the microcontroller to ensure the ratio and tolerances produce the expected result.

keyIdea.title: Dividers are for signals
keyIdea.text: Use voltage dividers to scale voltages for inputs, but do not use them as power supplies; buffer when the downstream load is significant.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.1 › Voltage Divider
Definition

Two resistors scale an input voltage

Formula: Vout = Vin × (R2 / (R1 + R2)). Useful for level shifting signals from 5 V sensors to 3.3 V inputs.
Worked example
Choose R1 = 10 kΩ, R2 = 20 kΩ with Vin = 5 V. Vout = 5 × (20 / 30) = 3.33 V, suitable for a 3.3 V input. Measure the result before connecting the microcontroller.
When to buffer
If the downstream input has low impedance or you need precise timing, add a buffer to avoid loading the divider and altering the voltage.
Do
Use dividers for signal scaling and measure before connecting.
Don't
Don't use a divider to power devices that draw current.
Key Takeaway
Voltage dividers are simple and effective for level shifting, but consider bufferization for loaded circuits.

screens.title: Breadboard Layout and Wiring Conventions
screens.narratorSegment: A breadboard is a reusable prototyping platform built from interconnected metal clips inside a plastic grid. The long horizontal strips along the edges are typically power rails — one for positive voltage and one for ground — and the short vertical groups in the middle are connected in groups of five holes. When you insert a component lead into a row of five, that lead is electrically connected to the other four holes in the same column. Always connect ground from your LaunchPad to the breadboard negative rail and power from the 3.3 volt or 5 volt pin to the positive rail as your design requires. Using color conventions for jumper wires — red for power, black or blue for ground — reduces wiring errors during assembly and troubleshooting. Common mistakes include placing component leads across different rows or forgetting to bridge a ground connection to the negative rail. When building the LED circuit, place the resistor in series with the LED so the current must pass through the resistor. Before powering the board, do a quick visual check: correct power rails, solid jumper connections, and no accidental shorts between adjacent rows. These small checks prevent damaging components when you apply power for the first time.

Module 2 › Chapter 2.1 › Breadboard Wiring
Overview

How rows and rails connect

Power rails run horizontally along edges. The central grid has vertical groups of five holes that are electrically common. Component leads and jumper wires share the same row when connected.

Practical wiring rules
  • Connect LaunchPad GND to the negative rail.
  • Connect 3.3 V or 5 V to the positive rail as needed.
  • Use red wires for power, black or blue for ground.
Assembly checklist
Confirm rail polarities, ensure resistor is in series with LED, and look for accidental shorts between rows before applying power.
Example: LED circuit layout
Place the LED so its anode connects to the resistor, the resistor connects to the 3.3 V rail or to a GPIO pin, and the cathode connects to ground rail. Verify continuity visually and with a meter if unsure.
Key Takeaway
Consistent placement and color conventions reduce wiring errors and make debugging faster.

screens.title: Build and Measure: LED with 220 Ω Resistor
screens.narratorSegment: Let's build the starter circuit and verify it with a multimeter. Step 1: place the LED on the breadboard so the anode and cathode occupy different rows. Step 2: insert the 220 ohm resistor in series with the anode lead, connecting the other end of the resistor to the 3.3 volt rail or to the LaunchPad GPIO pin you intend to use. Step 3: connect the cathode to the ground rail, and ensure the LaunchPad ground is tied to the breadboard negative rail. Step 4: power the board briefly and confirm the LED lights. Now measure: place the multimeter across the resistor and record the voltage drop; compute current with I = Vr / R. For example, if Vr reads about 1.3 volts across 220 ohms, I = 1.3 / 220 ≈ 0.0059 A or about 5.9 mA. That is a safe current for a GPIO pin within the typical 8 mA limit. A useful check is to also measure the LED forward voltage across the diode to confirm it is near the expected value, about 2 volts for a red LED. If measured currents exceed pin limits, power down, increase the resistor value, and test again. These measurement steps turn calculations into verified physical behavior.

screens.title: What to Remember
screens.narratorSegment: Keep these quick references in mind. First, standard voltages you will encounter: AA ≈ 1.5 volts, LaunchPad GPIO HIGH = 3.3 volts, USB = 5 volts. Second, safe current practice: small LEDs draw about ten milliamps and a typical microcontroller GPIO pin should be treated as roughly eight milliamps safe unless the datasheet states otherwise. Third, use conservative resistor choices: prefer the next larger standard resistor value when the calculated value is borderline, for example using 180 or 220 ohms instead of 162.5 ohms for an LED driven from 3.3 volts. These rules of thumb help you prototype quickly while limiting the chance of damage. When in doubt, measure the actual voltage and compute current using I = V / R to confirm behavior before running the system for long periods.

fullNarratorScript:
This chapter gives you the practical electrical vocabulary that makes embedded systems predictable and safe. You will learn what voltage, current, and resistance mean in physical terms, how Ohm's Law ties them together, and how resistors protect components like LEDs or translate voltages so sensors and microcontrollers can talk safely. We will use familiar examples — a single AA battery, the LaunchPad GPIO pins at 3.3 volts, and a USB five-volt supply — so you can map numbers to real hardware. You'll calculate currents through resistors, choose current-limiting resistors for LEDs, and build a simple breadboard circuit to measure voltages with a multimeter. That hands-on grounding prevents common mistakes like connecting an LED directly to a pin and risking damage. By the end of this lesson you will be able to compute voltage, current, or resistance from any two values, pick a safe resistor for an LED on a GPIO pin, and assemble and measure the circuit on a breadboard. Think of these skills as the electrical plumbing of your projects: they keep your system flowing without flooding the components.

Over the next segment you'll gain four practical competencies. First, you will be able to define voltage, current, and resistance in clear physical terms and explain how they relate through Ohm's Law; this matters because correct definitions prevent confusion between pressure and flow when you wire circuits. Second, you will learn to calculate any one quantity when given the other two; this calculation skill is useful in choosing parts and verifying designs before powering hardware. Third, you will understand resistor roles in embedded circuits, including current limiting for LEDs and voltage division for level shifting; that knowledge prevents burned-out LEDs and incorrect sensor readings. Fourth, you will physically build the LED circuit on a breadboard and use a multimeter to measure voltages and confirm expected currents; this hands-on practice tests theory against the real world. Each competency includes a small visual mnemonic so you can recall the relationships quickly, and every card ends with a verified competency milestone so you know when you've mastered the skill.

These objectives emphasize hands-on application and safety. You will practice calculating resistor values for LEDs using real numbers from a 3.3 volt GPIO pin and typical LED forward voltages. You will also learn to create a voltage divider that scales a five-volt sensor output to a 3.3 volt microcontroller input, including an example using ten and twenty kilohm resistors. The goal is not only to compute numbers but also to understand when a voltage divider is appropriate and when you must buffer the signal instead. Another practical objective is breadboard wiring and measurement: you will connect ground rails and power rails reliably, use color conventions for wires, and use a multimeter to measure voltage across components, then compute current from those measurements. Finally, you'll learn to respect the GPIO pin current limit — for the LaunchPad family that means keeping single-pin currents under about eight milliamps unless otherwise specified, and choosing larger resistors when necessary. These practical skills reduce the chance of damaging LEDs or the microcontroller when you prototype.

Voltage is the electrical potential difference between two points. Think of it as pressure in a water system: it is not the water flowing, but the push that can make water move when a path exists. In electronics we measure voltage in volts. Concrete examples help: a single AA battery typically supplies about 1.5 volts, the LaunchPad GPIO pins output 3.3 volts when HIGH, and a USB port provides 5 volts. Each of these numbers tells you how much potential energy per unit charge is available to move current through a component. A common misconception is to equate high voltage with high current — voltage is the driving force but only produces current when there is a path and a resistance. That distinction matters when you troubleshoot: a measured voltage at a pin does not guarantee a component will receive the expected current unless the circuit and resistor values are appropriate. In practice you use voltage to choose components and to determine expected drops across parts in series. For example, when driving an LED from 3.3 volts, we subtract the LED's forward voltage from the supply to determine how much voltage must appear across the resistor. Remember the water analogy: voltage sets the pressure, and it tells you how much potential there is to make things flow when the circuit is closed.

Current is the movement of electric charge through a conductor and is measured in amperes, commonly called amps. A practical way to think about current is water flow in a pipe: it tells you how much charge passes a point per second. Components consume current according to how they're designed — a small LED might draw ten milliamps, while a motor can draw hundreds of milliamps or several amps. Embedded systems are sensitive to current because microcontroller pins can only source or sink limited amounts; for example, the TM4C123G GPIO pins used on many LaunchPad boards can safely provide around eight milliamps per pin. Exceeding that limit risks overheating the chip or causing unreliable behavior. When designing circuits, always compute expected current flows using Ohm's Law and compare them to component limits. One common misunderstanding is to confuse current with the capacity of a power supply: a supply's voltage is fixed, but its available current depends on its rating and what the connected circuit draws. Practically, measure voltage across a resistor and divide by resistance to compute current if you cannot measure current directly. That verification step keeps prototypes safe and predictable.

Resistance measures how much a component opposes current. It is expressed in ohms and implemented with resistors — small components with a fixed resistance rating. In embedded work resistors are indispensable: they limit current so LEDs and pins are not overloaded, they form voltage dividers to scale signals, and they provide pull-up or pull-down behavior for inputs. For example, if you want about ten milliamps through a red LED with a roughly two-volt forward drop from a 3.3 volt pin, you compute the resistor as R = (3.3 − 2.0) / 0.01 ≈ 130 ohms. Because standard resistor values exist, you often pick the next common value, such as 150 or 220 ohms, which reduces the current and increases safety. A frequent mistake is to omit the resistor and connect an LED directly; an LED on its own has very low resistance when forward biased, so it will draw uncontrolled current, often damaging the LED and possibly the microcontroller pin. Resistances in series add; in parallel they divide, which matters when arranging resistor networks. Remember that resistors protect both the device that supplies current and the device that consumes it, so always include them where the design calls for controlled current.

Ohm's Law is the practical formula that links voltage, current, and resistance: V = I × R. It also rearranges to I = V / R or R = V / I. To solve real problems, start by identifying the known quantities and converting units so they match — for example, convert milliamps to amps when necessary. A step-by-step approach keeps you from introducing arithmetic errors: 1) write the formula for the unknown, 2) substitute numeric values with correct units, 3) compute, then 4) confirm the result against component limits. Concrete example: with a 3.3 volt output and a 220 ohm resistor, compute current as I = 3.3 / 220 ≈ 0.015 A or 15 mA. Compare that to the microcontroller pin limit; if the pin limit is 8 mA, you must increase the resistor value or use a driver. Watch out for unit mismatches — 0.015 A is 15 mA, not 0.015 mA. Another common error is forgetting that a resistor in series with an LED must take the voltage difference between supply and LED forward voltage. Always perform a final sanity check: does the computed current align with expected brightness or device heat? That final check prevents costly mistakes on the bench.

When you drive an LED from a microcontroller pin, the resistor in series is the safety mechanism. The calculation uses the LED forward voltage and desired current: R = (Vsource − Vforward) / I. For example, with 3.3 volts from a GPIO pin and a red LED forward voltage around 2.0 volts, aiming for 10 milliamps gives R ≈ 130 ohms. In practice, pick the nearest common resistor value such as 150 or 220 ohms to reduce current slightly and preserve the pin. A key safety check is to compare the computed current to the microcontroller's per-pin limit — on some LaunchPad devices that limit is roughly 8 milliamps per pin. If the computed current exceeds the limit, increase the resistor value or use a transistor driver to source the LED current instead of the pin. Another point to compare is brightness versus safety: higher current makes a brighter LED, but pins and LEDs have thermal limits. A typical mistake is to assume any low-value resistor is fine because the supply voltage is small; even small supplies produce harmful current without proper resistance. Use the resistor to control current, verify by measuring voltage across it, and compute current using I = Vr / R to confirm.

A voltage divider is two resistors in series that produce an output voltage equal to the input scaled by the ratio of the lower resistor to the total: Vout = Vin × (R2 / (R1 + R2)). It’s a simple and common way to step a 5 volt signal down to 3.3 volts so a microcontroller input isn’t overdriven. For example, selecting R1 = 10 kilohms and R2 = 20 kilohms with a 5 volt input yields Vout = 5 × (20k / (10k + 20k)) = 5 × (20/30) = 3.33 volts, close to the 3.3 volt target. When using dividers, be mindful of the input impedance of the receiving pin and any dynamic behavior of the sensor: voltage dividers present a finite output impedance that can be loaded down by low-impedance inputs or by sampling circuits at high speed. For sensors that drive significant current or require accurate timing, buffer the divider output with an op-amp or a voltage follower. A common misconception is to assume a divider can power a load — dividers are for signal scaling, not supplying current. Always measure the scaled voltage with a meter before connecting to the microcontroller to ensure the ratio and tolerances produce the expected result.
